Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters US-Israel war on Iran US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran Washington launches campaign to isolate Tehran but it is unclear whether it will apply measures to China Julian Borger Senior international correspondent Mon 24 Aug 2026 14.57 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 18.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US has threatened to impose severe sanctions against any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran , hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do. It is unclear, however, how far the Trump administration is prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally. Iran, meanwhile, vowed retaliation against any country that took part in the US-led isolation campaign. Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war. “Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” Bessent said on Monday. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.” Asked whether sanctions would be applied to China, which bought an estimated 80% of Iran’s shipped oil last year, he replied: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions. That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.” Bessent said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances. “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.” Bessent said Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the ​Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem. China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.” Tehran said it would retaliate against the sanctions using a range of measures. Maj Gen Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces’ chief of staff, said the retaliation could take the form of land, sea or air operations or cyber-attacks. The announcement of secondary sanctions against Iran comes nearly six months after the the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ali Khamenei. Early expectations that the regime in Tehran would collapse or agree to Washington’s demands to give up uranium enrichment and other key elements of its nuclear programme were dashed. Hardliners appeared to strengthen their grip on government in Tehran and responded by declaring the closure of the strait of Hormuz, attacking ships that ignored its declaration. Trump imposed a counter-blockage on Iranian oil exports through the strait, leading to an impasse that has had profound effects on the global economy. Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said: “After nearly six months without a military or diplomatic victory, Washington appears to be trying to accomplish through intensified economic strangulation what military force has so far failed to achieve. But Tehran is answering that zero-sum approach with one of its own.” The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, however, said further military action was not off the table. “By no means are we foreclosing using ‌kinetic strikes anywhere in the ​strait of Hormuz or around Iran,” Hegseth ⁠told reporters on Monday. In apparent anticipation of the US measures, the United Arab Emirates, a close US and Israeli ally, announced it was suspending trade ties with Iran. Turkey, another trading partner with Iran, which has been critical of the US-led campaign against the Islamic Republic, has yet to respond to the US threat of sanctions. Andrew Miller, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said: “The announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran and those countries trading with it signals what is plain to all: this war has brought the United States no closer to eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme or crippling the Iranian regime. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Germany Suspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Bavaria About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany Donna Ferguson and agencies Sat 24 Oct 2026 06.04 EDT First published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 02.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google German police have arrested a suspect after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed. About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany . Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said. “A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the fire. Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000 feet). The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said. Built by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”, according to its website . It is only accessible via a road cut into the mountain through previously impassable terrain. Nazis would enter a tunnel and take a 124-metre golden brass lift buried in the mountain to get inside the building. Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.15pm (7.50pm), police said. When firefighters arrived on the scene at about 9.50pm, the entire building was engulfed in flames. No reason for the fire was given, but the German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson. Firefighters found no one inside the building, which was reportedly still burning at 7am on Saturday – more than nine hours after the alarm was raised. View image in fullscreen A photograph from 2007 of the Kehlsteinhaus, or Eagle's Nest, near Berchtesgaden, Germany. Photograph: Geir Moulson/AP Fire departments from six municipalities sent emergency personnel to tackle the blaze and the Bavarian Red Cross, the local mountain rescue service and the police also attended the incident. Later that morning, the blaze appeared to be out, although smoke continued to rise from the smouldering building. A police spokesperson told the German tabloid Bild: “It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved.” Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an AFP photographer. Maier said police were still investigating and would hold a news conference later on Saturday. According to Bild, a motorcyclist whom local police officers came across on their way to the scene had been arrested, but his involvement in the fire remains unclear and a police spokesperson declined to release information about his identity. The Eagle’s Nest was constructed between 1937 and 1938 and forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists in the Holocaust. It became legendary in the postwar period and was often depicted as an essential meeting place in US war films, although in reality Hitler rarely visited the complex. The building survived the second world war undamaged and since 1952 has hosted an exhibition by the Institute for Contemporary History recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant.
